name: Houses of Learning and Lost Libraries
description: From clay tablets in Nineveh to the reading rooms of Alexandria and Oxford: how people gathered, lost and guarded books and teachers for three thousand years.

checkpoints.name: Ancient collections
checkpoints.note: The first libraries were royal collections of tablets and scrolls. Plato's Academy trained thinkers, Alexandria gathered the books of the known world, and Nalanda in India drew students from across Asia.

checkpoints.name: Schools of the Islamic world and Europe
checkpoints.note: In Baghdad the House of Wisdom translated the learning of many peoples, while al-Qarawiyyin and al-Azhar taught the faithful. In Europe, Bologna, Oxford and Paris began as guilds of students and masters.

checkpoints.name: The medieval universities
checkpoints.note: Cambridge, Salamanca and Prague spread the university across Europe. The Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258, destroying its great libraries, and the Popes built a new library at the Vatican.

checkpoints.name: Libraries and universities, modern
checkpoints.note: The Bodleian, Harvard and the Library of Congress made collecting books a national task. Tokyo brought Western learning to Japan, and Alexandria's new library, opened in 2002, recalls the lost one.
